fullText:
Super interesting finding on optimizing agent harnesses.

When you optimize an agent harness for both quality and cost, apply your cost preference only at the end of the search, since applying it at every step throws away harnesses that lead to better ones.

That is the key insight behind Microsoft's ParetoSaddler.

At each step, an optimizer edits a parent harness. Both versions run several times, and a Bayesian bootstrap over those runs decides whether the candidate shows credible progress in quality or in cost. Promoted candidates stay available as parents, and the final deployment choice is made separately.

On GAIA2, quality goes from 56.22% to 62.89% while cost per task drops from $0.78 to $0.45. On ClawMark, quality goes from 70.86% to 81.35%, and cost drops from $1.17 to $1.01.

The Pareto-selected harnesses also beat quality-only optimization on both quality and cost.

If your harness search only tracks accuracy, add repeated runs and a cost axis before deciding which candidates to keep.

generally the ability for products and services to differentiate with technology is increasing much more rapidly than the diffusion of those technologies across incumbent service providers.

@united uptake of @Starlink (to which I owe this 250mbps connectivity) versus @Delta feet-dragging is a fine example.

@Tesla FSD a more dramatic one.

The future is here--as they say--it's just unevenly distributed.

This is typically accompanied by a picture of an F35 buzzing some bedouins on camels. 

With the implication being that the lack of diffusion is a function of societal, geographic and cultural distance.

Perhaps it were once so. 

The curve of technology has steepened so precipitously, however, that now the uneven distribution is appearing in companies, products and services occupying nearly identical shelf space, or populating neighboring garages.

You may find yourself flying an F35 while your neighbor tries to convince his camel to gallop down the driveway.

A marginal change in the innovation uptake within a company can now quickly and radically compound into almost unrecognizably different services. With each time step the distance grows.

Tesla now occupies an entirely different product category from its long-reputed killers. (Remember the Model S killers, and the Model 3 killers, and the Model Y killers; alas they have mostly themselves died.) 

Comparing Siri to ChatGPT, Grokbot, and Muse is like comparing a pocket calculator to a smartphone.

From the consumer side this means a seemingly marginal change can radically improve the quality of the service you receive. As consumers acclimate, and increasingly use AI agents to aggressive guide their choices, business dynamism will correspondingly increase.

The laggards will get weeded out as consumers vote with their dollars.

Across industries I would expect that you will see ahistoric share-shifts as well as accelerating business concentration.

Markets new and old will be put increasingly up for grabs and will be more likely to submit to winner-take-most mechanics once they have been latched onto by a company with sufficiently deepening innovation pace.

(Welcome to the singularity; we're glad you made it.)

Great paper from Alibaba on self-evolving agents, with a live A/B test across 200,000+ merchants.

(bookmark it)

This is another brilliant example of leveraging episodic memory with agents and the importance of attribution.

SPAR runs B2B sales outreach on Alibaba's 1688 platform. Conversion rose 15.8%, and high-intent merchant growth rose 35.8%.

The agent learns at two levels without updating weights. An inner loop keeps episodic memory for each merchant across sessions. An outer loop maintains a shared playbook of selling strategies, each written as a testable hypothesis.

The key step is attribution. Before changing the playbook, SPAR decides whether a lost deal came from a bad strategy or an outside factor, so a deal lost to outside factors doesn't change a strategy that works.

Domain experts rated it 4.62 out of 5 on sales quality, the highest of all methods tested.

If you are building agents that learn from production outcomes, it might be worth adding an attribution step before writing any lesson to memory.

fullText:
Impressive paper from Stanford on harness evolution for robotics.

They improve frozen robot policies from 9.7% to 43.3% success on unseen scenes without changing a single weight.

The gain comes from the harness.

RoboArchitect gives a coding model the robot's rollouts. The coding model diagnoses failures and rewrites the control code around the frozen policy. That code decides when to call the policy, when to use vision tools and when to command the arm directly.

The harness is optimized on one set of episodes and tested on held-out scenes and tasks. Success on unseen tasks rises from 12.7% to 40.2%.

The largest gains appear where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data. Inside an evolved harness, a general-purpose policy often beats the finetuned version of the same policy.

The search also produced control routines such as lifting a jammed arm clear, and it added a persistent memory that stores values like effective grasp depths.
